clue.text: Bit depressed, it's extremely painful

parts.note: a whit is a tiny bit, as in 'not a whit'
low means depressed, down in spirits

explanation.surface: Someone feeling a little down announces that something hurts badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit depressed' reads as one phrase about mood, but it splits into two pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A whitlow is an infected swelling at a fingertip, known for being acutely sore.

clue.text: He will give expression of triumph in Spain about hospital, unbearable place

indicators.note: the joined words go round the hospital abbreviation, so about means surrounding here

parts.note: contracted, he will is written he'll
ole is the Spanish cry of triumph heard at bullfights
H is the standard abbreviation for hospital on road signs and maps

explanation.surface: A man promises to cheer Spanish-style around a hospital in a dreadful place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks as if it applies only to the Spanish cry, but it is the whole of 'He will' plus that cry that goes round the hospital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A hellhole is a slang term for a wretched, intolerable spot to live or be.

clue.text: Sad football team?

explanation.surface: A football side that has lost is described as down in the dumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the blues means feeling melancholy; the Blues is also the nickname of clubs such as Chelsea and Everton, who play in blue.

clue.text: Sick of having no variety

explanation.surface: Someone is unwell from a monotonous diet of the same thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes sorts literally: being out of sorts means having run out of kinds or varieties.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling out of sorts is an idiom for being slightly unwell; literally it means lacking any sorts, that is kinds.

clue.text: Plant female goes without, we hear

indicators.note: the phrase tells us the letters come from how the words are spoken, not written

parts.note: F for female plus lacks, meaning goes without, is spoken just like the plant

explanation.surface: A woman goes without, according to rumour, while a plant is mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: F (female) and LACKS (goes without) together are spoken exactly like the plant name.
explanation.definitionFit: Flax is a blue-flowered crop grown for linen fibre and linseed oil.

clue.text: Well-wisher to finish after half a day

indicators.note: after places the word for finish behind the first piece
only half of the day's name is kept, the second three letters being dropped

parts.note: Friday is a day of the week
end means finish

explanation.surface: A kindly person waits to clock off once half the day is gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half a' keeps the first half of the day's name, and 'after' puts the word for finish behind it; the day is Friday.
explanation.definitionFit: A friend is someone who wishes you well, a supportive companion.

clue.text: Herod was a tenacious chap, it was reported

indicators.note: reported signals that the words are to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: a tenacious chap is a gripper, one who holds on tight

explanation.surface: Gossip has it that King Herod was a man who would not let go.
explanation.walkthrough: Herod Agrippa was a king of Judaea in the New Testament; 'a gripper', said in a non-rhotic accent, is heard as his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Herod Agrippa was the Roman-era king of Judaea named in the Acts of the Apostles.

clue.text: Scramble young fish and cook rapidly in pan

parts.note: to stir is to mix, as when scrambling eggs
fry are newly hatched fish

explanation.surface: A kitchen instruction: mix up some baby fish and fry them fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scramble' and 'cook' make it look like an egg recipe, but scramble just gives STIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Stir-frying is the wok method of cooking small pieces fast over high heat.

clue.text: You can be sure of that being OK

definitions.text: You can be sure of that

explanation.surface: Someone reassures us that a thing is definitely fine.
explanation.definitionFit: As an emphatic tag ('he'll come, all right') it means certainly; as a reply it means acceptable or fine.

clue.text: Former prince annexing a province

parts.note: Albert, consort of Queen Victoria, was a prince of the past

explanation.surface: A long-dead royal takes over a region.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Albert was Queen Victoria's husband. 'annexing' only joins the two pieces, A being tacked on after ALBERT.
explanation.definitionFit: Alberta is one of Canada's prairie provinces, named after Princess Louise Caroline Alberta.

clue.text: Old man finished early, about ten, outside

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: 'Old man finished early, about ten, outside' (EXTERIOR). EX (old man) and X or IO (ten) fit, but no reading of 'finished early' and 'about' gives the remaining letters; exact-text searches found no source or parse.
annotationWithheld.clue: Old man finished early, about ten, outside

clue.text: French capture on board?

parts.note: a French phrase meaning in passing, which also names a pawn-taking move in chess, the board being a chessboard

explanation.surface: A seizure in France made aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' suggests a ship, but it means on a chessboard.
explanation.definitionFit: The en passant rule lets a pawn take an enemy pawn that has just advanced two squares beside it.

clue.text: Gurkha lifted section for Islamic leader

indicators.note: a section is a part cut from something, so the letters are a run taken from inside the two words

explanation.surface: Part of a Nepalese soldier's kit is raised for a Muslim ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' tempts as a reversal signal, but the run reads forwards across GurKHA LIFted.
explanation.definitionFit: A khalif (caliph) was the successor of Muhammad as civil and religious ruler of Muslims.

clue.text: Marvellous rhyme

explanation.surface: Praise for a fine bit of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Super-duper is jokey slang for excellent, and it is itself a rhyming pair of words.

clue.text: Mood of one in front of mirror?

definitions.text: Mood of one in front of mirror?

parts.words: Mood of one in front of mirror?
parts.note: a pensive, thoughtful frame of mind, which is also literally what a mirror is to anyone standing before it

explanation.surface: How someone feels as they stand gazing at a looking-glass.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means thoughtful, but also describes giving back an image, which is what the person gets from the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Being reflective means being deep in thought, and a mirror's surface is reflective in the optical sense.

clue.text: Feel disposed to take flight

indicators.note: disposed can mean arranged or set out, so the letters of feel are set out afresh

explanation.surface: Someone is inclined to run away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feel disposed' reads as 'be inclined', but 'disposed' signals the letters of FEEL rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To flee is to run off from danger, escaping fast.

clue.text: Disturbing force not quite holding as much as possible

parts.note: stress is a pressure or force acting on something

indicators.note: not quite tells us to drop the final letter, leaving the word a touch short

parts.note: full describes a container with as much in it as it can take

explanation.surface: Unsettling pressure falls just short of maximum capacity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' trims FULL to FUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stressful causes worry and strain, unsettling the person facing it.

clue.text: Poorly balanced piles, odd arrangement

indicators.note: an arrangement is a new ordering, so the letters of the two previous words are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Stacks that are unevenly built make a strange display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' looks like an adjective describing the arrangement, but it is part of the letters reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: Lopsided means leaning to one side, with weight unevenly spread.

clue.text: Scientifically impersonal type of thermometer

explanation.surface: A detached, scientific attitude is compared to a medical instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Clinical can mean coolly detached and efficient; a clinical thermometer is the kind used to take body temperature.

clue.text: Article on shopping centre in London

parts.note: the is the definite article in grammar
a mall is an enclosed shopping centre

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about a London shopping arcade.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mall is the ceremonial avenue running from Trafalgar Square to Buckingham Palace in London, not a shopping centre at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The thoroughfare known by this name is the grand processional road leading to Buckingham Palace in London.

clue.text: Spoils putting nearly everything on a wine

parts.note: mars means spoils or damages

indicators.note: nearly says the word is used minus its last letter

parts.note: all means everything

explanation.surface: Someone ruins things by staking almost all they have on one bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting ... on' only joins the pieces; 'nearly' cuts ALL to AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Marsala is a fortified dessert wine from Sicily.

clue.text: Nothing I left you started was greasy

parts.note: O, the round figure zero, stands for nothing

indicators.note: started points to the beginning of the word you, so only its first letter is used

explanation.surface: Someone confesses that what they left you had begun to turn greasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'you started' means the start of 'you', a Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Oily means covered in or soaked with fat, slick and slippery.

clue.text: These areas cultivated to produce garden flower

indicators.note: cultivated soil is worked and turned over, so the letters of these areas are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Tilled beds yield a bloom in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cultivated' fits the gardening picture but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartsease is the wild pansy, a small violet-family plant grown in borders.

clue.text: Jack and Diana south found it was more spacious inside than expected

definitions.text: it was more spacious inside than expected

parts.note: a jack or jack tar is a sailor, so Jack gives tar
Di is the short form of the name Diana
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Two people head south and discover a deceptively roomy place.
explanation.walkthrough: The TARDIS is the time machine in the BBC series Doctor Who, a police box far bigger inside than out.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor Who's time-travelling police box is famously bigger within than its exterior suggests.

clue.text: No end of money in old place for gambling

indicators.note: no end of says the word loses its final letter

parts.note: cash means money

explanation.surface: Endless amounts of money were staked at an old gaming venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of money' sounds like 'masses of money', but it cuts CASH to CAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A casino is an establishment where people play roulette, cards and other games for stakes.

clue.text: Doubt that water vapour will cause corrosion

parts.note: mist is fine water vapour hanging in the air
rust is the corrosion of iron

explanation.surface: Someone worries that moisture in the air will make metal decay.
explanation.definitionFit: To mistrust is to be suspicious of or lack confidence in someone.

clue.text: The course in which one might get into difficulties

definitions.text: The course in which one might get into difficulties

parts.words: The course in which one might get into difficulties
parts.note: a dish served as a meal course, and the idiom of being in it means being in trouble

explanation.surface: A route or path where trouble could arise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' suggests a route or study course, but it is a course of a meal; being 'in the soup' is British slang for being in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Soup is a starter course, and 'in the soup' is an idiom for facing trouble.

clue.text: Half-a-dozen beside a channel bridge

parts.note: six is VI in Roman numerals
a duct is a channel or pipe for fluid

explanation.surface: Six sit beside a waterway crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beside' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A viaduct is a long bridge on many arches carrying a road or railway over a valley.

clue.text: Land with very small population according to the book

definitions.text: Land with very small population according to the book

parts.words: Land with very small population according to the book
parts.note: a country in a Swift novel inhabited by tiny people only six inches tall

explanation.surface: A sparsely peopled country, according to a written account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very small population' suggests few people, but means the people themselves are tiny; the book is Gulliver's Travels.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's island in Gulliver's Travels is peopled by miniature folk, and its name now means anything tiny.

clue.text: Prepared to accept the Italian without delay

indicators.note: to accept means to take in, so the first word holds the second inside it

parts.note: ready means prepared
il is Italian for the

explanation.surface: Someone is willing to welcome the Italian at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Italian' is the Italian definite article, a common crossword device for foreign words meaning 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Readily means promptly or willingly, with no hesitation.
